analogy.p: Think of the seven diseases as seven suspects in a police file, each with a type (virus, bacterium, fungus, protist), a method (how it gets in), a calling card (symptoms) and a way to stop it. If you can fill in all four columns for each suspect you can answer any question. It breaks down because real pathogens can share methods (two diseases may both spread by air) so do not assume a pattern from one example.

bullets: **Viral**: measles, HIV/AIDS, TMV (plant).
**Bacterial**: salmonella (food poisoning), gonorrhoea (STD).
**Fungal**: rose black spot (plant).
**Protist**: malaria (spread by mosquito vector).
For each know: **cause, symptoms, spread, prevention/treatment**.
Know which affect plants (TMV, rose black spot) and which affect people.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.3.1 requires you to know named examples of viral, bacterial, fungal and protist diseases and, for each, **the symptoms, how it is spread, and how it is treated or controlled**. The diseases are **measles, HIV and tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)** (viral), **salmonella and gonorrhoea** (bacterial), **rose black spot** (fungal) and **malaria** (protist). You must also explain how spread of each can be reduced or prevented. Examiners love these because they are pure recall plus application.

bullets: **Virus**: not a cell; reproduces only inside host cells; measles, HIV, TMV.
**Bacterium**: single cell without a nucleus; divides rapidly; salmonella, gonorrhoea.
**Fungus**: hyphae and spores; rose black spot.
**Protist**: single-celled with a nucleus; malaria (Plasmodium).
Bacteria make you ill by damaging cells and by releasing **toxins**.
Viruses damage the cells they reproduce in, often bursting them.
Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses; fungicides kill fungi.
Some pathogens infect people (measles, HIV) and some infect plants (TMV, rose black spot).
core.p: A **pathogen** is a microorganism that causes disease, and the specification groups the examples into four types. **Viruses** are not cells at all: they are tiny particles of genetic material inside a protein coat, and they can only reproduce inside the cells of a living host, which they damage. **Bacteria** are single-celled organisms with no nucleus that divide quickly in the warm, nutrient-rich conditions of the body and may release **toxins** that make you ill. **Fungi** may be single-celled or made of long threads called **hyphae**, and they spread by spores. **Protists** are mostly single-celled organisms with a nucleus, and some are parasites that live in a host and need a vector to move between hosts. Knowing the type tells you which treatment can work.

bullets: Cause: measles virus, which reproduces inside cells.
Symptoms: **fever** and **red skin rash**.
Spread: **droplets from coughs and sneezes** breathed in (air).
Serious complications can lead to death, so prevention matters.
Prevention: **vaccination** of young children (MMR), which gives herd immunity when enough people are immune.
Antibiotics do not work because it is viral.
core.p: **Measles** is a viral disease. Its symptoms are **a fever and a red skin rash**. It is spread by **inhalation of droplets from coughs and sneezes** of an infected person, so it passes very easily in crowded places such as schools. Measles is serious, and can be **fatal if complications arise**, for example pneumonia or swelling of the brain. For this reason **most young children are vaccinated against measles** in the UK (the MMR vaccine).

bullets: Early stage: **flu-like illness**.
Later: the immune system is attacked and weakened.
AIDS: so badly damaged the body cannot fight **other infections or cancers**; it is these that cause illness and death.
Spread: **sexual contact**; **sharing needles** (blood); also mother to baby.
Treatment: **antiretroviral drugs**, which **prevent the virus from replicating** inside the body.
Prevention: condoms, not sharing needles, screening donated blood.
core.p: **HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)** infects and destroys **white blood cells**, especially helper T lymphocytes, which weakens the immune system. Initially HIV causes **flu-like symptoms** for a short time. The virus then stays in the body, and if untreated it can lead to **AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome)**, in which the immune system is so badly damaged that it **cannot deal with other infections or cancers**. HIV is spread by **sexual contact** or by **exchange of body fluids such as blood**, which happens when drug users share needles.

bullets: Symptom: **mosaic** (patchy light and dark) pattern on leaves.
Why growth falls: **photosynthesis is reduced**, so fewer sugars for growth.
Spread: by contact between plants, on hands or tools, and by insects (vectors).
Control: remove and destroy infected plants, control insect vectors, use clean tools, plant resistant varieties.
It is a virus, so fungicides and antibiotics do not work.
Reduces crop yield, a food security issue.
core.p: **TMV** is a widespread plant pathogen that infects many plants, including tomatoes and tobacco. It gives a distinctive **mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves**. The discoloured parts of the leaf **cannot carry out photosynthesis** because the virus destroys the chloroplasts, so **less glucose is made and plant growth is reduced**. There is no cure once a plant is infected.

bullets: Symptoms: **fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea**.
Cause: bacteria and the toxins they produce.
Spread: **contaminated food** (poor hygiene, undercooked meat, raw eggs).
Control: **vaccinating poultry**, cooking food thoroughly, washing hands, separating raw and cooked foods.
Storing food at the right temperature stops bacteria multiplying.
Danger: dehydration, especially for the very young and old.
core.p: **Salmonella** food poisoning is caused by bacteria. Symptoms are **fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea**, caused by the bacteria and the **toxins** they secrete. It is spread by **eating food contaminated with salmonella bacteria**, for example because of poor hygiene during food preparation, or because the food (such as poultry, eggs) came from infected animals. In the UK, **poultry are vaccinated against salmonella** to control the spread.

bullets: Symptoms: **thick yellow/green discharge** and **pain when urinating**.
Spread: **sexual contact**.
History: penicillin used to work, now **resistant strains**.
Resistance arises by natural selection: bacteria with resistance survive and reproduce.
Prevention: **condoms** (barrier methods); screening and treating partners.
Link: antibiotic resistance and the need for new antibiotics.
core.p: **Gonorrhoea** is a **sexually transmitted disease (STD)** caused by bacteria. Symptoms are a **thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis** and **pain on urinating**. It is spread by **sexual contact**. It was once easily treated with **penicillin**, but **many resistant strains have appeared**, so penicillin no longer works for these. Treatment is with other antibiotics, but spread is prevented using **barrier methods of contraception such as condoms**.

bullets: Symptoms: **purple/black spots**, leaves turn **yellow** and fall early.
Effect: less leaf area, **less photosynthesis**, **reduced growth**.
Spread: **wind and water**.
Control: **fungicides**, **strip and destroy** infected leaves (do not compost them).
Spacing plants out reduces spread by water splash.
Antibiotics will not work on fungi.
core.p: **Rose black spot** is a fungal disease of rose plants. **Purple or black spots** develop on the leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. Because the leaves are damaged, **photosynthesis is reduced**, which affects the **growth** of the plant. It is **spread in the environment by wind or water**, such as rain splashing spores from leaf to leaf. Gardeners treat it using **fungicides** and/or by **stripping off the affected leaves and destroying them** so the fungus cannot spread.

bullets: Cause: a **protist** (not a bacterium or virus).
Vector: **mosquito**; it is not harmed but carries the protist.
Symptoms: **recurrent fever** and it can be **fatal**.
Control: stop **mosquito breeding** (drain standing water, insecticides) and use **bed nets**.
Also: insect repellent, antimalarial drugs for travellers.
Common mistake: malaria is **not** spread directly from person to person.
core.p: **Malaria** is caused by a **protist** (Plasmodium). The protist has a **life cycle that includes the mosquito**, which is a **vector**: it carries the pathogen from one host to another. When a mosquito bites an infected person it takes up the protist, and when it bites another person it passes the protist on. Malaria causes **recurrent episodes of fever** and can be **fatal**. The spread is controlled by **preventing the vectors (mosquitoes) from breeding** and by using **mosquito nets** to avoid being bitten.

bullets: Air: measles. Contact/body fluids: HIV, gonorrhoea. Food: salmonella. Wind/water: rose black spot. Vector: malaria.
Vaccination used for: measles, salmonella (in poultry).
Antibiotics used for: gonorrhoea, salmonella severe cases; never viruses.
Antiretrovirals: HIV only.
Fungicides: rose black spot.
Vector control: malaria.
core.p: Examiners often give a table or ask you to compare diseases. Sort them by pathogen, route of spread and control. Notice the patterns: air droplets (measles), body fluids and contact (HIV, gonorrhoea), contaminated food (salmonella), wind and water (rose black spot), and a vector (malaria).

bullets: Always link: route → control → why it works.
Herd immunity: when most are vaccinated, spread is limited even to unvaccinated people.
Remove the source: infected leaves, contaminated food, standing water.
Break the chain: vector, hand washing, cooking.
Resistance means treatment may fail, so prevention is vital.
Cost and practicality may feature in 6-mark evaluate questions.
core.p: Strong answers link the **method of control to the route of spread**. Vaccination stops measles because immune people cannot be infected and cannot pass it on. Condoms stop sexually transmitted diseases because they form a physical barrier to body fluids. Killing mosquito larvae prevents malaria because it removes the vector. Destroying leaves removes the source of fungal spores.

bullets: Photosynthesis: damaged leaves cannot make glucose.
Evolution: resistant gonorrhoea strains, natural selection.
Immune system: HIV attacks white blood cells.
Ecology: vectors and parasites.
Reproduction: STDs and barrier contraception.
Food security: plant diseases reduce yields.
core.p: These examples are used throughout 4.3: spread and prevention, human defence systems (white blood cells, antibodies), vaccination, antibiotics and painkillers (why they do not work on viruses) and evolution (antibiotic resistance in gonorrhoea). The plant examples link to photosynthesis in 4.4 and to food security in ecology.

bullets: Describe the trend: 'cases fell from 2000 to 200 between 1990 and 2000'.
Percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100; a fall gives a negative value.
Explain a fall in measles cases using vaccination and herd immunity.
For HIV graphs: T cell count falls as virus numbers rise; AIDS is the late stage.
Use data from both axes and quote units (cases, years).
Compare diseases using one clear point each: pathogen, spread, control.
A schematic graph shows a typical pattern, not measured data.
Do not say a graph 'proves' something unless the evidence is strong enough.
core.h: Reading data and graphs about disease
core.p: Exam questions often give a table or graph of numbers of cases, such as measles cases before and after a vaccination programme, or HIV levels over time, and ask you to describe or explain the pattern. Describe first, using figures from the data with units, then explain using the biology. For a graph, state the overall trend, quote values at two points, and calculate a change or percentage change if asked. A drop in cases after vaccination is explained by more people being immune, so fewer people can pass the disease on (herd immunity). Be careful not to claim that a correlation proves a cause unless the question gives enough evidence.

exam: **State (1 mark)** the pathogen type: e.g. malaria = protist; rose black spot = fungus; measles = virus; salmonella = bacterium.
**Symptoms questions**: give two linked symptoms from the spec, e.g. fever and red rash (measles).
**Spread questions**: name the route precisely: droplets from coughs and sneezes; sexual contact; body fluids; contaminated food; wind and water; mosquito vector.
**Control questions (2 marks)**: method + how it works, e.g. nets stop mosquitoes biting.
**Explain why growth is reduced in infected plants (2 marks)**: leaf damaged, less photosynthesis, less glucose.
**Gonorrhoea**: mention resistance to penicillin and the use of condoms.
**HIV 3 marks**: virus attacks immune system, antiretrovirals stop replication, AIDS leaves body unable to fight other infections.
**Compare diseases (4 marks)**: use one pathogen type or route per sentence; keep each comparison explicit.
**Use data**: from a table of cases, compare numbers before and after vaccination.
**Graph question (3 marks)**: describe the trend with figures and units, then explain it with biology (vaccination, immunity, vector control).
**Prevention versus treatment**: prevention stops infection (vaccines, nets, hygiene); treatment deals with an existing infection (antiretrovirals, antibiotics, fungicides).

mistakes.r: Malaria is caused by a protist; the mosquito is the vector that spreads it.
mistakes.w: Malaria is caused by a mosquito.

mistakes.r: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the late stage when the immune system is badly damaged.
mistakes.w: HIV and AIDS are the same thing.

mistakes.r: They are viral; antibiotics do not work. HIV is treated with antiretroviral drugs.
It is a fungal disease; it is treated with fungicides.
mistakes.w: Rose black spot is caused by bacteria.

mistakes.r: Measles is spread by inhaling droplets from coughs and sneezes.
It is spread by eating contaminated food.

mistakes.w: Gonorrhoea can still always be cured with penicillin.

mistakes.r: They are a barrier that prevents contact with infected body fluids.
mistakes.w: Condoms stop gonorrhoea by killing bacteria.

mistakes.r: Vaccines prevent infection by making the person immune beforehand; treatment uses drugs such as antiretrovirals or antibiotics.
mistakes.w: Vaccines treat people who already have the disease.

mistakes.r: Viruses are not cells; they can only reproduce inside living host cells.

summary: AQA expects you to know, for measles, HIV, TMV, salmonella, gonorrhoea, rose black spot and malaria, the type of pathogen, the symptoms, how each is spread and how it is treated or its spread reduced. These are among the most frequently examined recall questions in the infection and response topic.

terms.d: A viral disease with fever and a red skin rash, spread by droplets from coughs and sneezes.
Human immunodeficiency virus, which attacks the immune system.
Acquired immune deficiency syndrome: the stage where the immune system is so badly damaged it cannot deal with other infections or cancers.
Drugs that prevent HIV from replicating inside the body.
A plant virus causing a mosaic pattern of discolouration on leaves.
Bacteria that cause food poisoning: fever, cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea.
A sexually transmitted disease caused by bacteria, with thick yellow or green discharge and pain on urinating.
A disease spread by sexual contact.
A fungal disease causing purple or black spots on leaves.
A disease caused by a protist, spread by mosquitoes, causing recurrent fever.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another.
A form of bacteria that is no longer killed by an antibiotic.
Contraception such as a condom that prevents body fluids passing between partners.
A pattern of discoloured patches on a leaf.
The organism a pathogen lives in or on and harms.
The thin threads that make up the body of a fungus.

worked.ans: Symptoms include fever, stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea (2). Spread can be reduced by vaccinating poultry against salmonella (1) and by good hygiene and cooking food thoroughly to kill bacteria (1).
worked.q: Salmonella food poisoning is caused by bacteria. Describe the symptoms and explain how its spread to people can be reduced. (4 marks)
steps: Symptoms (up to 2): fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea.
Reduce spread (up to 2): vaccinate poultry; cook food thoroughly; hygiene during preparation.

worked.ans: Remove and destroy the infected leaves (1) so the fungus cannot spread to other leaves/plants by wind or water (1). Use a fungicide to kill the fungus (1).
worked.q: A gardener has rose black spot on their roses. Explain what they should do and why. (3 marks)
steps: Strip off affected leaves and destroy them: removes fungus so it cannot spread by wind/water.
Result: leaves can photosynthesise so plant grows.

worked.ans: Nets prevent mosquitoes biting people (1), so the protist that causes malaria cannot be passed on from the mosquito to the person (1).
worked.q: Explain why mosquito nets reduce the number of people with malaria. (2 marks)
steps: Mosquito is the vector that passes on the protist.
